## Abstract

### Background

 PacBio high fidelity (HiFi) sequencing reads are both long (15–20 kb) and highly accurate (> Q20). Because of these properties, they have revolutionised genome assembly leading to more accurate and contiguous genomes. In eukaryotes the mitochondrial genome is sequenced alongside the nuclear genome often at very high coverage. A dedicated tool for mitochondrial genome assembly using HiFi reads is still missing.

### Results

 MitoHiFi was developed within the Darwin Tree of Life Project to assemble mitochondrial genomes from the HiFi reads generated for target species. The input for MitoHiFi is either the raw reads or the assembled contigs, and the tool outputs a mitochondrial genome sequence fasta file along with annotation of protein and RNA genes. Variants arising from heteroplasmy are assembled independently, and nuclear insertions of mitochondrial sequences are identified and not used in organellar genome assembly. MitoHiFi has been used to assemble 374 mitochondrial genomes (368 Metazoa and 6 Fungi species) for the Darwin Tree of Life Project, the Vertebrate Genomes Project and the Aquatic Symbiosis Genome Project. Inspection of 60 mitochondrial genomes assembled with MitoHiFi for species that already have reference sequences in public databases showed the widespread presence of previously unreported repeats.

### Conclusions

 MitoHiFi is able to assemble mitochondrial genomes from a wide phylogenetic range of taxa from Pacbio HiFi data. MitoHiFi is written in python and is freely available on GitHub ([https://github.com/marcelauliano/MitoHiFi](https://github.com/marcelauliano/MitoHiFi)). MitoHiFi is available with its dependencies as a Docker container on GitHub (ghcr.io/marcelauliano/mitohifi:master).

## Background

Recent advances in genomics have opened the prospect of full genome sequencing of a wide range of species. Both global and taxonomically- or geographically-bounded projects have been initiated to exploit these new technologies to build reference genome libraries for all species on Earth. It is expected that these genome sequences will be a foundational dataset for new understanding in biology, new avenues in conservation and biodiversity monitoring, and new data to promote sustainable bioindustry \[[1](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR1 "Richards S. It’s more than stamp collecting: how genome sequencing can unify biological research. Trends Genet TIG. 2015;31:411–21."), [2](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR2 "Blaxter M, Archibald JM, Childers AK, Coddington JA, Crandall KA, Di Palma F, et al. Why sequence all eukaryotes? Proc Natl Acad Sci. 2022;119:2115636118.")\]. The Earth Biogenome Project (EBP) \[[3](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR3 "Lewin HA, Robinson GE, Kress WJ, Baker WJ, Coddington J, Crandall KA, et al. Earth biogenome project: sequencing life for the future of life. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2018;115:4325–33.")\] was founded to coordinate and promote biodiversity genomics through affiliated projects such as the Darwin Tree of Life project (DToL) \[[4](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR4 "Blaxter M, Mieszkowska N, Di Palma F, Holland P, Durbin R, et al. Sequence locally, think globally: the darwin tree of life project. Proc Natl Acad Sci. 2022;119:e2115642118.")\], the Vertebrate Genomes Project (VGP) \[[5](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR5 "Rhie A, McCarthy SA, Fedrigo O, Damas J, Formenti G, Koren S, et al. Towards complete and error-free genome assemblies of all vertebrate species. Nature. 2021;592:737–46.")\] and the Aquatic Symbiosis Genomics project (ASG) \[[6](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR6 "Aquatic symbiosis genomics project - Wellcome Sanger Institute [Internet]. [cited 2022 Sep 6]. Available from: 
https://www.sanger.ac.uk/collaboration/aquatic-symbiosis-genomics-project/
")\]. DToL is geographically-focussed, and aims to sequence all eukaryotic species living in and around the islands of Britain and Ireland. The goals of VGP are taxonomically-oriented (to sequence all vertebrate species), while those of ASG are defined by a particular biology (eukaryotes that live in symbiosis with prokaryotic or eukaryotic microbial partners). For each of these and other EBP projects, extensive development is needed in sample collection and preservation, nucleic acid extraction, sequencing, assembly, curation and annotation. A key driver in all these fields is the development of processes that can work at scale, processing hundreds to thousands of species rapidly.

One key advance has been the release of commercial long read sequencing platforms. Here we focus in particular on the PacBio zero mode waveguide, single molecule real time sequencing technology, and the particular deployment of this approach to produce long, high-quality reads using a circular consensus approach (called HiFi for high fidelity). These data have N50 read lengths of 15–20 kb, and accuracies higher than 1 error in 100 (Q20). This radically new data type has changed the landscape of genome assembly \[[7](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR7 "Wenger AM, Peluso P, Rowell WJ, Chang P-C, Hall RJ, Concepcion GT, et al. Accurate circular consensus long-read sequencing improves variant detection and assembly of a human genome. Nat Biotechnol. 2019;37:1155–62.")\], and new toolkits (such as HiCanu \[[8](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR8 "Nurk S, Walenz BP, Rhie A, Vollger MR, Logsdon GA, Grothe R, Miga KH, Eichler EE, Phillippy AM, Koren S. HiCanu: accurate assembly of segmental duplications, satellites, and allelic variants from high-fidelity long reads. Genome Res. 2020;30(9):1291–305.")\] and HiFiAsm \[[9](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR9 "Cheng H, Concepcion GT, Feng X, Zhang H, Li H. Haplotype-resolved de novo assembly using phased assembly graphs with hifiasm. Nat Methods. 2021;18:170–5.")\]) have been developed to exploit the characteristics of HiFi data.

Except for a few groups, all eukaryotes carry an essential cytoplasmic organelle, the mitochondrion. The mitochondrion derives from an ancient symbiosis between the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes and an alphaproteobacterial cell, and while many genes that were on the ancestral bacterial genome have been transferred to the nuclear genome \[[10](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR10 "Lane N, Martin W. The energetics of genome complexity. Nature. 2010;467:929–34.")\], the mitochondrion generally retains a reduced, circular genome \[[11](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR11 "Gray MW, Burger G, Lang BF. Mitochondrial evolution. Science. 1999;283:1476–81.")\]. Mitochondria play a fundamental role in aerobic respiration and other key processes and the genes on the mitochondrial genome are essential for these functions \[[12](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR12 "Wallace DC. Mitochondrial DNA in evolution and disease. Nature. 2016;535:498–500.")\]. While mitochondrial genome content varies extensively \[[13](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR13 "Formaggioni A, Luchetti A, Plazzi F. Mitochondrial genomic landscape: a portrait of the mitochondrial genome 40 years after the first complete sequence. Life. 2021;11:663.")\], in Metazoa the gene content of the mitochondrial replicon is relatively stable (11 or 12 protein coding genes, two ribosomal RNAs and a set of tRNAs that decode the distinct organellar genetic code). Because the mitochondrial genome is haploid, and generally passes only through the maternal lineage, drift and linked selection tend to purge variants rapidly. Heteroplasmy, the presence of variant mitochondrial genomes within a single individual, has been thought to be generally rare and often associated with disease or normal somatic ageing processes. Although repeats have been reported in mitochondrial genomes \[[14](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR14 "Formenti G, Rhie A, Balacco J, Haase B, Mountcastle J, Fedrigo O, et al. Complete vertebrate mitogenomes reveal widespread repeats and gene duplications. Genome Biol. 2021;22:120.")\], the extent of the phenomenon is not fully understood. For example, the assembly and analysis of PacBio CLR and ONT sequencing data identified widespread repeat content and frequent heteroplasmy in vertebrate mitochondrial genomes \[[14](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR14 "Formenti G, Rhie A, Balacco J, Haase B, Mountcastle J, Fedrigo O, et al. Complete vertebrate mitogenomes reveal widespread repeats and gene duplications. Genome Biol. 2021;22:120.")\]. These features were not evident in, or accessible through, previous short-read or PCR-and-sequence approaches.

The increase in the rate of generation of reference genomes across biodiversity using accurate long reads offers an opportunity to revisit the evolution of the gene content and structure of mitochondrial genomes. This opportunity requires development of robust pipelines that reliably assemble organellar genomes, correctly report repeat content, resolve heteroplasmy and distinguish true mitochondrial genome sequence from the frequent presence of nuclear genome inserted copies (nuclear mitochondrial transfers or NUMTs). Here we present MitoHiFi, a software designed to use Pacbio HiFi reads to assemble and annotate complete mitochondrial genomes. MitoHiFi was developed within the Darwin Tree of Life Project and has been deployed to assemble mitochondrial genomes from hundreds of Metazoa and Fungi. MitoHiFi is distributed under the MIT licence, and is available on GitHub ([https://github.com/marcelauliano](https://github.com/marcelauliano)) and as a Docker container also on GitHub (ghcr.io/marcelauliano/mitohifi:master).

## Results

### MitoHiFi is a robust toolkit for mitochondrial genome assembly from HiFi data

MitoHiFi is written in python and orchestrates a series of external tools to select mitochondrial reads from whole genome sequencing datasets, filter out reads that are likely to derive from nuclear-mitochondrial transfers (NUMTs), assembles the genome, circularising it when possible and annotate it for protein and RNA genes. MitoHiFi also identifies possible heteroplasmic variants present in the data (Fig. [1](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#Fig1)). We describe the processes embodied in MitoHiFi below.

**Fig. 1**

![Fig. 1](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12859-023-05385-y/MediaObjects/12859_2023_5385_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y/figures/1)

Outline of the MitoHiFi workflow. Flow diagram of MitoHiFi processes. The inputs to MitoHiFi are a closely-related reference mitochondrial genome with either (i) raw Pacbio HiFi reads (−r parameter), or (ii) previously assembled contigs (−c parameter). Example of outputs generated by MitoHiFi. A summary of the outputs generated by the pipeline, including the contigs\_stats.tsv table summarising the metrics for the assembly, output sequence and annotation files, and graphical representations of coverage and annotation

#### Selection of PacBio HiFi reads based on reference mitochondrial genome(s) from closely-related species

As primary input, MitoHiFi takes Pacbio HiFi reads (-r flag), or contigs assembled from those reads (-c), and a reference mitochondrial genome from a closely-related species along with its annotation in GenBank format. The pipeline includes a script to automatically download closely-related mitochondrial genomes based on the NCBI taxonomy (findMitoReference.py). The defaults are set to download a single reference genome from the same or most-closely related species, but multiple references can be downloaded by setting -n (> 1). When MitoHiFi is starting from reads (-r), it first maps the reads to this reference mitochondrial genome. The aligned read set is filtered to exclude reads that have lengths more than the exact length of the reference genome, as these are likely to derive from NUMT insertions. However, this parameter can be changed when appropriate (*flag –max-read-len*).

#### Assembly of mitochondrial reads and filtering of contigs to avoid NUMTs

The readset is then assembled with Hifiasm \[[9](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR9 "Cheng H, Concepcion GT, Feng X, Zhang H, Li H. Haplotype-resolved de novo assembly using phased assembly graphs with hifiasm. Nat Methods. 2021;18:170–5.")\] and assembled contigs are parsed through a series of filters to yield final mitochondrial genome candidates. The contigs are compared to the reference mitochondrial genome using BLAST + \[[15](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR15 "Camacho C, Coulouris G, Avagyan V, Ma N, Papadopoulos J, Bealer K, et al. BLAST+: architecture and applications. BMC Bioinform. 2009;10:421.")\]. Contigs are retained if.

1.  i.
    
    Over 50% of their sequence length is present in the BLAST match with the reference (the user can change this threshold with the flag *\-p*).
    
2.  ii.
    
    The contig is less than five times the length of the reference (long contigs are likely to be NUMTs).
    
3.  iii.
    
    The contig is > 80% of the length of the reference (smaller contigs are likely to be incomplete).
    

All BLAST parsing information is saved in intermediate files *parsed\_blast.txt* and *parsed\_blast\_all.txt* (see GitHub page for intermediate output column details).

#### Circularization

All candidate contigs are processed through circularizationCheck \[[16](/article/10.1186/s12859-023-05385-y#ref-CR16 "Allio R, Schomaker-Bastos A, Romiguier J, Prosdocimi F, Nabholz B, Delsuc F. MitoFinder: efficient automated large-scale extraction of mitogenomic data in target enrichment phylogenomics. Mol Ecol Resour. 2020;20:892–905.")\]. This module uses self-BLAST of each contig to identify sequence redundancy between its ends. ## Abstract

### Importance:

The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in excess mortality among the general US population and at Veterans Health Administration (VHA) facilities. It is critical to understand the characteristics of facilities that experienced the highest and lowest pandemic-related mortality to inform future mitigation efforts.

### Objective:

To identify facility-level excess mortality during the pandemic and to correlate these estimates with facility characteristics and community-wide rates of COVID-19 burden.

### Design:

We used pre-pandemic data to estimate mortality risk prediction models using 5-fold cross-validation and Poisson quasi-likelihood regression. We then estimated excess mortality and observed versus expected (O/E) mortality ratios by the VHA facility from March to December 2020. We examined facility-level characteristics by excess mortality quartile.

### Participants:

Overall, there were 11.4 million VHA enrollees during 2016 and 2020.

### Main Measures:

Facility-level O/E mortality ratios and excess all-cause mortality.

### Result:

VHA-enrolled veterans experienced 52,038 excess deaths from March to December 2020, equating to 16.8% excess mortality. Facility-specific rates ranged from −5.5% to +63.7%. Facilities in the lowest quartile for excess mortality experienced fewer COVID-19 deaths (0.7–1.51, *P* < 0.001) and cases (52.0–63.0, *P* = 0.002) per 1,000 population compared with the highest quartile. The highest quartile facilities had more hospital beds (276.7–187.6, *P* = 0.024) and a higher percent change in the share of visits conducted via telehealth from 2019 to 2020 (183%–133%, *P* < 0.008).

### Conclusions:

There was a large variation in mortality across VHA facilities during the pandemic, which was only partially explained by the local COVID-19 burden. Our work provides a framework for large health care systems to identify changes in facility-level mortality during a public health emergency.

**Keywords:** Covid-19, mortality, predictive modeling, Veterans Health Administration

---

The Veterans Health Administration (VHA) is the largest health care system in the US and provides care to millions of veterans through a network of medical centers and affiliated outpatient clinics.[1](#R1) The VHA began preparing for the COVID-19 epidemic in January 2020 and has since implemented robust national measures to reduce the spread of the virus within VHA Medical Centers.[2](#R2),[3](#R3) These include screening and testing for COVID-19, mandatory staff training, triaging care for infected Veterans, and the provision of telehealth services for those not infected.[3](#R3),[4](#R4) Notably, there were widespread cancellations of elective admissions and referrals to specialty care that allowed to maintain availability for those affected by COVID-19.[5](#R5) These strategies to reduce viral transmission while maintaining critical access to health services were supported by guidance promulgated by the US Centers for Disease Control and World Health Organization.[6](#R6) Perhaps as a result of these measures, the VHA experienced a 42% reduction in inpatient admissions and a 30% reduction in outpatient visits during the pandemic’s early months.[7](#R7),[8](#R8) During the same time period, telehealth appointment volume grew rapidly, especially for mental health.[9](#R9) While the VHA was able to scale up telehealth, some high-value services (eg, foot exams for diabetics, medication-assisted therapy for opioid use disorder, and cervical cancer screenings) may have been delayed or forgone entirely during this period.[10](#R10) Delayed or avoided care has been associated with increased mortality among both Veterans and the general population.[11](#R11),[12](#R12)

In prior work, VHA compared favorably to the US general population in estimates of excess all-cause mortality rates from March to December 2020 (16.7% vs. 22.9%).[13](#R13),[14](#R14) However, these national-level estimates potentially mask substantial facility-level variation and are insufficient for performance management within the VHA or other integrated health systems. Previous studies have focused on facility characteristics associated with COVID-19 outcomes at nursing homes and assisted living communities.[15](#R15),[16](#R16) A systematic review found that larger medical facilities and facilities in an area with high COVID-19 prevalence were the strongest predictors of high COVID burden.[17](#R17) During the peak of the pandemic, many larger VA facilities saw an influx of transfers from surrounding VA and non-VA facilities that had less capacity to treat severe COVID-19 illness.[18](#R18) To our knowledge, there have been no studies that examined variation in excess mortality among VHA facilities.

The objectives of this study were to estimate excess mortality at individual VHA facilities (defined as medical centers and their affiliated outpatient clinics) and to validate these estimates against measures of COVID-19 burden within the facility’s catchment area. We also examined facility characteristics that may be associated with increased facility-level excess mortality, including hospital size, rurality, clinical complexity, staffing levels, appointment capacity, and telehealth utilization. Our work provides valuable insights not only for institutional learning at the VHA, but other large health care systems, to forecast changes in mortality, identify facilities that perform better or worse than predicted, and learn from it by further identifying facility risk factors that may be associated with increased vulnerability during a public health emergency.

## METHODS

### Data and Study Population

We queried administrative data for 11.4 million unique veterans who were enrolled in the VHA and were engaged in care during 2016 and 2020 using the VHA’s Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW). Data included individual-level demographics, priority group (an eligibility determination based on service-connection disabilities, household income, and other selection criteria), and individual comorbid conditions. We used a 1-year look back period to assign Quan-Elixhauser comorbidities as of January 1st in each calendar year.[19](#R19) The death data used includes all deaths that occurred, both within and outside the VHA system. VHA’s death data rely on multiple sources, including government death certificates and the Social Security Administration. Death records were obtained from 3 VHA data holdings: the S-patient table in the VHA CDW, the Vital Status Mini, and the Master Veteran Index. Facility characteristics included the number of hospital beds, percentage of rural enrollees, Clinical Complexity (an index that considers the patient population, clinical services complexity, and education and research at a facility),[20](#R20) number of staff, appointment capacity, and relative percent change in telehealth usage (volume of outpatient care delivered through telehealth divided by the total volume of outpatient care from 2019 to 2020). The percentage of rural enrollees was defined by using patient-level data provided by the VA Planning Systems Support Group (PSSG), which maintains a quarterly file of enrollee addresses. We assigned veterans to the nearest VHA facility and then for each facility, calculated the share of veterans that reside in urban counties based on the US Census Bureau classifications. Appointment capacity was defined as the total number of hours from the start of a provider’s first clinical encounter through their last encounter each day, summed across all providers throughout the year. County-month-level data on confirmed COVID-19 cases and deaths among the US general population were extracted from the Johns Hopkins Coronavirus Resource Center.[21](#R21) Our unit of observation was the facility month.

### Statistical Analysis

Our analysis proceeded in 5 steps. We first used 10-fold cross-validation to divide pre-pandemic data (2016–2019) into training and test sets.[14](#R14) Second, we estimated a mortality prediction model on the training sets using a Poisson quasi-likelihood regression model based on previous work, with the log of Veterans assigned to each facility as the offset.[14](#R14) The model included dummy variables for respondent’s age category (55–64, 65–79, 80+), service-connected disability (priority groups 1–4), low-income (priority groups 5 & 7), houselessness (identified using ICD-10 codes Z59.0 or Z59.1), and individual Quan-Elixhauser comorbidities,[19](#R19) with fixed effects for month and facility. These latter effects were intended to capture seasonality in deaths and time-invariant facility-level characteristics. The estimated coefficients were averaged across folds. Third, we used the test sets to assess model performance using both median squared error and calibration slope. Fourth, we generated regression predictions for each facility month from March to December 2020 and divided the observed mortality by predicted mortality to estimate observed versus expected (O/E) death ratios. Excess deaths were calculated by subtracting observed deaths from expected deaths. We divided O/E ratios into quartiles, correlated them with facility-level characteristics and measures of COVID-19 burden (confirmed cases and deaths) within the facility’s catchment area, and used a 2-tailed *t*\-test to compare the lowest and highest quartiles. Lastly, we ran bivariate regressions of O/E and COVID-19 deaths and cases to determine the percent variation explained by local COVID-19 conditions. Catchments were defined as a weighted average of counties based on the proportion of a facility’s patients that resided in each county. We chose this definition over other arbitrary geographic boundaries, such as county or state, as these catchment areas are defined based on actual patient flows versus arbitrary administrative boundaries. Moreover, our research question focuses on how individual facilities performed during the pandemic. All analyses were conducted using Microsoft *R* Open version 4.0.2 (Redmond, WA).

## RESULTS

A total of 11,428,134 veterans were engaged in care from the VHA between 2016 and 2020 ([Table 1](#T1)). We observed 1,511,101 all-cause deaths between 2016 and 2019 and 426,069 all-cause deaths in 2020. Overall, veterans who died in 2020 were slightly older compared with the Veterans who died in prior years; the share of 65- to 79-year-old deceased veterans rose from 29.8% in 2016–2019 to 32.3% in 2020. There was a slight shift in racial/ethnic composition among the deceased. In particular, the share of deceased Black Veterans increased from 7.9% in 2016–2019 to 9.2% in 2020 (χ[2](#R2): 3673,15, *df*\= 5, *P* < 0.001).

## 结果

### 管线性能

MitoHiFi 从 DToL（350 种）、VGP（22 种）和 ASG（2 种）项目共组装了 374 个线粒体基因组，涵盖 39 个后生动物目及 6 个真菌物种。组装结果已提交至 INSDC 或 VGP GenomeArk 数据库。真菌线粒体基因组组装大小范围为 43–133 kb。Hifiasm 在 MitoHiFi 内部经常组装出多个候选线粒体基因组，这可能是由于 reads 错误和高覆盖率或真实的异质性所致。

### 与已发表参考序列的比较

在 60 个可与 INSDC 数据库比对记录进行比较的物种中，大多数物种的组装体大小相近，核苷酸一致性超过 96%。只有 3 个 MitoHiFi 组装体比已发表参考序列更小。其中，*Flammulina velutipes* 的 MitoHiFi 组装体较数据库参考 (JN190940.1) 短 8927 bp。将 HiFi reads 比对至这 8 kb 序列以及对该序列在 NCBI 核苷酸数据库中进行 BLAST 搜索，均未找到支持其存在的证据，该区段亦不含必需保守基因。

16 个 MitoHiFi 组装体大于其先前版本。核苷酸一致性和基因内容检查显示，重复序列是组装体变长的原因。以 *Tridacna gigas* 和 *Tridacna crocea* 为例，两者组装体均存在三类重复，但在 MitoHiFi 组装体中重复拷贝数更多，且这些重复由 HiFi 数据支撑。在这些较大组装体中，比对区域的核苷酸一致性始终超过 95%。

MitoHiFi 在原始 reads 输入时性能最优，因为该模式使工具能够有效排除源自 NUMTs/NUPTs 的 reads，并利用长度阈值识别可能的 NUMT/NUPT 组装位点。当前使用相对宽松的长度截断值，因为既往短读长或 PCR 方法可能压缩了重复区域，导致真实基因组长度被低估。对 MitoHiFi 输出的检查表明这些过滤策略在排除 NUMTs/NUPTs 方面有效（Additional file 4: Figure S2），但工具同时保留了全部候选组装体输出，以便在不满足预期参数时进行人工验证。

该工具的主要局限体现在植物细胞器基因组上。由于植物线粒体和叶绿体基因组的大小、基因含量和重复组成在不同物种间差异显著，且大型重复区域可能超过单条 HiFi read 的长度，MitoHiFi 目前无法完全解析这些结构。目前建议对所有植物细胞器组装结果进行人工检查和手动校正。开发工作正致力于引入基于组装图 (graph-based) 的方法，利用大 k-mer 尺寸来跨越重复区段，以更完整地呈现植物细胞器基因组的异构体结构。

---

## 结论

MitoHiFi 是一个可从广泛系统发育范围物种的 PacBio HiFi 数据中高效组装和注释线粒体基因组的工具，已成功应用于 374 个物种的组装。该工具识别出已发表参考序列中存在广泛重复序列的局部缺失，并通过长读长 HiFi 数据提供了更完整的组装。MitoHiFi 使用 Python 编写，以 MIT 许可证在 GitHub 上公开发布，同时提供 Docker 容器。
